task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: how to isolate lineup effect on shot mix
how to measure shot mix change
sample size and power for lineup analysis
measure reliability of shot type classification
own_inferences: No prior evidence retrieved; the question of whether changing the offensive lineup alters shot mix has not been directly addressed in the available historical record. The data set is large (three seasons of NBA regular season and playoffs) but the complexity of lineup permutations and the need to control for multiple confounders suggest the analysis will be methodologically challenging. Based on these considerations, the question is likely to be difficult to answer definitively with the current data set. The probability of obtaining a statistically powerful test is modest because many lineup combinations will have few observations, and the effect size of personnel on shot mix may be small relative to noise. Potential confounders (defensive matchup, game context, offensive tempo) may not be fully captured by the available variables. This inference is not drawn from any retrieved record.
uncertainties: Exact magnitude of personnel effects on shot mix; availability of adequate covariates to fully capture defensive matchup; distribution of lineup combinations and resulting sample sizes per combination.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was found, so the decision is based solely on methodological considerations.

blocking_constraints.text: Many lineup combinations will have few observations, reducing power.
Shot type classification from play-by-play may be noisy.
Unobserved defensive and contextual factors could bias estimates.
Substitution rotation intervals may not capture rapid lineup changes.
Large number of lineup comparisons increases risk of false positives.

prior_work.summary: No prior work addressing this specific question was retrieved.

risks.text: Defensive matchup and game context not fully captured.
Many lineup comparisons increase false discovery risk.

design.estimand: Effect of offensive lineup composition on shot mix (percentage of shots by distance/shot type).
design.sample: All possessions in NBA 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular season and playoffs where lineup is known.
design.power: Not feasible with current data due to low sample sizes per lineup; power likely <80% for small effect sizes.
design.controls: Defensive matchup minutes, game context (score differential, period), offensive tempo estimates, player usage rates.
design.falsification: Test for lineup effect on a randomized outcome (e.g., random assignment of a dummy variable to lineup) to check for model misspecification.
design.multiplicity: Apply false discovery rate control across all lineup comparisons.
design.decision_rule: Reject the hypothesis if p<0.05 after FDR correction; otherwise fail to reject.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular season and playoffs per-game play-by-play and substitution data.
